In the waiting room

It's 19 February 2035, 3 in the morning, in the maternity ward of the hospital where Mara works. Mara is in the delivery room. Jakob has come out into the corridor for five minutes. Ludwig has come by taxi, even though everyone told him not to.
Jakob. How is she?
Fine. Very fine. Everything's completely normal. The midwife says it'll take a few more hours. I'm completely calm.
Son, you're pretending to be calm. But your jacket's on inside out.
What? Oh. Oh no. Since when?
Since you left home, I suppose. Sit down. You look as if you hadn't slept for three nights.
Two. She's been having contractions since the day before yesterday. Ludwig, why are you here? It's three in the morning. You're eighty-six.

Exactly. Maybe I won't have many more chances to wait for a baby at the hospital at night. In 1975 I waited for Thomas. In 1980 for Sabine. Back then fathers weren't allowed inside. We sat in the corridor and pretended to read the paper.
And what was it like? When you first saw Thomas?
As if someone had put the world in my hands. A very small world that screamed very loudly. And I was scared of dropping it.
That's exactly what I'm scared of. I hold her and it's as if I were holding a soap bubble.
That passes. After three weeks you hold her as if you'd never done anything else. And now turn your jacket round. Your daughter mustn't think her father can't dress himself.
Daughter? We don't even know if it's a girl.
I know. Ingrid told me. In a dream. Last night.

1. als ob / als wenn + Konjunktiv II
An unreal comparison says how something SEEMS, even though it isn't so (or we don't know if it is). You use Konjunktiv II, verb at the end:
He's pretending to be calm. (but he isn't)
“als ob” and “als wenn” mean exactly the same thing. “als ob” is more common.
2. The short version: als + verb
You can leave out “ob / wenn”. Then the conjugated verb comes RIGHT AFTER “als”:
With als ob (verb at the end)
With als (verb straight after)
…, als ob er ruhig wäre.
…, als wäre er ruhig.
…, als ob er nicht geschlafen hätte.
…, als hätte er nicht geschlafen.
…, als ob die Zeit stehen bleiben würde.
…, als würde die Zeit stehen bleiben.
Don't mix them: “als ob wäre er ruhig” ✗. Either “als ob er ruhig wäre” or “als wäre er ruhig”.
3. Present or past in the comparison
Time relationship
Konj. II present (wäre, hätte, würde + Inf.)
Er sieht aus, als ob er müde wäre.
Konj. II past (hätte / wäre + Part.)
Er sieht aus, als ob er nicht geschlafen hätte.
The tense of the main clause doesn't matter: “Er sah aus, als ob er müde wäre” (past + unreal present = simultaneous in the past).

Ingrid Hilde

Ingrid Hilde Lorenz came into the world on the nineteenth of February 2035, at twelve minutes past six, in a delivery room on the third floor of the hospital where her mother had worked for eight years. She weighed three thousand two hundred grams, was fifty-one centimetres long and, as the midwife immediately noted, had a surprisingly powerful voice. Outside it was still dark. It was snowing softly, for the first time in February, and the flakes drifted past the big windows as if the city were welcoming her with a white curtain.

The birth had taken a long time. Two days and two nights, since the first contractions had started on Friday evening, in the middle of dinner at Lena and Andrei's on the first floor, when Mara suddenly put her fork down and said: “I think it's starting.” Jakob had gone pale, as if he had seen a ghost. Andrei had fetched the car. Lena had fetched the bag that had been standing packed by Mara's door for three weeks. And Ludwig, downstairs on the ground floor, had heard the noise on the stairs, opened his door and shouted: “Good luck!”, so loudly that Fritz started barking. Then the house went quiet. Nobody really slept that night.

The midwife was called Mrs Okonkwo; she had worked at the hospital for twenty years and knew Mara well, because they had often sat together in the canteen. She laid the baby on Mara's chest, still wet, still screaming, with tiny wrinkled hands that moved in the air as if they were looking for something. Mara held her tight. She didn't say anything. She just looked at her daughter, for a long time, with a face on which exhaustion and happiness were so mixed that Mrs Okonkwo said later that in twenty years she had seen a thousand mothers, but never one who looked as if she had run a marathon and met an angel at the same time.

Jakob stood beside the bed, his jacket finally the right way round, and cried without noticing. When Mrs Okonkwo put the baby in his arms, wrapped in a white blanket, he held her as carefully as if he were holding a soap bubble and as stiffly as if he were afraid to move. Ingrid Hilde stopped crying. She opened her eyes, very briefly, dark blue, like all newborns, and looked at her father, or seemed to look at him, and Jakob said later that it was as if she already knew him. As if she were saying: oh, it's you. Good. Then everything's all right.

Ludwig was still sitting in the corridor, on a hard plastic chair, with his walking stick between his knees and the old brass bell in his jacket pocket. He hadn't slept all night. A young nurse who knew Mara had brought him tea twice and a blanket once, and asked him whether he wouldn't rather go home. Each time he had shaken his head. “I sat on a chair like this in 1975,” he had said. “And once more in 1980. And in 2002, when my granddaughter was born, in Potsdam. I know how to wait.”

At half past six the door opened and Jakob came out. He looked as if he hadn't slept for three days, which was almost true, and at the same time as if he had won the lottery. He sat down next to Ludwig on the second plastic chair and said nothing for a while. Then he said a single word: “A girl.” And then, after a pause: “You were right. Ingrid was right.” Ludwig nodded slowly. He wanted to say something, but he couldn't. He just put his old hand on Jakob's knee, and that's how they sat, two men in a hospital corridor at half past six in the morning, while it snowed outside, and neither of them said anything, and it was as if they had never understood each other better.

Then Ludwig, very slowly, took the old brass bell out of his jacket pocket. Jakob looked at it and laughed softly. “Not here, Ludwig,” he said. “It's a hospital.” Ludwig nodded. He didn't ring the bell. He just held it in his hand, tightly, the whole time, the way you hold a lucky charm. “I know,” he said. “I'll ring it at home. When she comes into the house for the first time. Once. For Ingrid.”

An hour later Ludwig was allowed in. Mara was sitting in bed, exhausted, her cheeks red, and in her arm, in the white blanket, was a tiny face with closed eyes and a little tuft of black hair. “Ludwig,” Mara said softly. “May I introduce her to you? Ingrid Hilde.” Ludwig came slowly up to the bed, leaning on his stick, and looked at the baby for a long time. Then Mara said: “Do you want to hold her?” Ludwig shook his head. “I'm eighty-six,” he said. “My hands shake.” “That's exactly why,” said Mara. “Sit down. I'll pass her to you.”

He sat down on the chair beside the bed, and Mara put the baby in his arms, very carefully, and Ludwig's hands stopped shaking. Just like that. As if they remembered how it's done. He held Ingrid Hilde the way he had held Thomas in December 1975, Sabine in May 1980 and Lena in the autumn of 2002. She weighed almost nothing. She smelled of milk and of something new that had no name. And when, in her sleep, she closed her little hand around his finger, the old, crooked finger that had pressed the controller of a tram for forty-one years, he looked as if someone had put the world in his hands. For the fourth time in his life.

In the afternoon the others came. Lena and Andrei, with flowers and a cake that nobody ate. Elena and Dan from Sibiu, who had taken the first flight in the morning after Andrei had called them at half past six, and who looked as if they had run all the way. Mrs Lorenz from Thuringia, with a baby romper suit she had knitted herself, in a green that Mara secretly found hideous and later used every day. And in the evening, when most of them had gone, someone else came, in a wheelchair, pushed by Elif: Grete Hoffmann, ninety-eight, in black, with her pearl necklace, who had insisted on coming even though Mrs Petersen from the care home had forbidden it.
Mara had slept for a few hours in the meantime, with the baby on her chest, and with her hair combed and a clean nightdress she looked almost like herself again.

Grete had herself pushed up to the bed and looked at the baby for a long time, with her clear, ironic gaze, which now wasn't ironic at all. Then she stretched out her thin old hand, the hand that had played the piano for ninety years, and touched the tiny fingers very lightly. “Long fingers,” she said. “Very long fingers. That's a pianist, Mara. You can see it straight away.” Mara laughed. “Mrs Hoffmann, she's twelve hours old.” Grete looked at her as if Mara had said something very silly. “So what?” she said. “Mozart was twelve hours old once too. I'll take her at six. Wednesdays at four. Elif can teach her the scales until I'm back.” Nobody asked where Grete meant to go. Everyone pretended not to have heard.

Dan had stood silently by the window the whole time, with his granddaughter in his arms; he had hardly put her down since he arrived. He didn't speak German, and Grete didn't speak Romanian, but when she looked at him, he said something to Andrei, and Andrei translated: “Dad says you're right. The baby has a pianist's hands. But she gets her voice from my sister. And her stubbornness.” Grete laughed, for the first time that evening, a clear, surprised laugh. “Tell your father,” she said, “that you need stubbornness for the piano. Otherwise you give up after the first scale.”

Late at night, when Jakob had fallen asleep on a folding chair next to Mara's bed and the baby was lying in her cot, Mara looked out of the window at the snow-covered city. She thought of a young nurse from Sibiu who had come to a foreign city eight years ago with a suitcase and a dictionary, thinking she would stay two years to earn money and then go back home. She thought of the stairwell on Kastanienallee, of an old man with a dog who had shown her the way to the third floor. It seemed like yesterday. And at the same time like another life. Ingrid Hilde stirred in her sleep and made a little sound, like a sigh. And Mara knew she was home.

Five days later, Mara and Jakob brought their daughter home to Kastanienallee thirty-one. It was a cold, clear Saturday morning, the snow was still lying on the roofs, and in front of the front door stood the whole house: Lena and Andrei, Kuba and Ola with their parents, the Yilmaz family from next door, Mrs Schulze with her walking frame, and Fritz, who was very old and very slow and still wagged his tail. And in the doorway, leaning on his stick, stood Ludwig. When Jakob carried the baby seat up the three steps to the door, Ludwig took the old brass bell out of his pocket and rang it. Once. Loud and clear. For Ingrid. And the baby in the seat, who had been asleep until then, opened her eyes as if she had been waiting for exactly that sound.
